articles.title: macOS 26.7 Code Hints at Two Unreleased Apple Game Controllers
articles.subtitle: References to two unreleased controllers that identify as Apple hardware in code were spotted in the macOS 26.7 release candidate by MacRumors reader Pdfu.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
References to two unreleased controllers that identify as Apple hardware in code were spotted in the macOS 26.7 release candidate by MacRumors reader Pdfu. Apple's first macOS 26.7 release candidate came out in mid-August, and it was full of references to unreleased Apple devices, from iPhones and Macs to new home accessories. Pdfu has continued to dig into the RC, finding new details that were previously overlooked.

There are GameController profiles for two hardware devices identified as T6502 and T1057, which Pdfu suggests could be Apple gaming controllers in development. The two controllers have different haptic designs and standard controller components, like a D-pad, dual thumbsticks, shoulder buttons, Home and Menu buttons, and analog triggers. T1057 also has accelerometer and gyroscope support, while T6502 doesn't.

The code includes dedicated hardware plug-ins for each device as well, which suggests these are actual devices instead of placeholder code.

There have been rumors about a possible Apple game controller over the years, but nothing has ever materialized.

The code found in the first macOS Tahoe 26.7 RC could point to an Apple controller in the works, but it could also be referencing internal test hardware Apple uses for testing game controller code and support. Apple removed the code in the second ‌macOS Tahoe‌ 26.7 RC.

Apple has had multiple opportunities to release a game controller. The company could have launched one alongside any version of the Apple TV, when Apple Arcade came out, or when the Vision Pro launched, but it didn't. Instead, Apple focused on building extensive support for third-party controllers.

In 2015, Apple required ‌Apple TV‌ games to support the Siri Remote as a gaming controller, but gave that up in a matter of months. With the Vision Pro, it partnered with Sony to add Vision Pro support to the PlayStation VR2 Sense controllers instead of designing its own controller.

Console makers have mastered the controller, and many people already have Xbox, PlayStation, or Nintendo controllers. There's little improvement to be made on controller ergonomics, but if Apple is working on a controller, features like Find My and instant cross-device pairing could set it apart from competitors.

All of the references can be found in blacktop/ipsw-diffs on GitHub, with Pdfu's highlights available in the forum post.

articles.title: Apple’s China AI strategy now includes training its own custom model, per report
articles.subtitle: china Apple Intelligence Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
china

Apple Intelligence

Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.

Reuters reports that three sources described the China-specific model as a departure from Apple’s strategy of relying on third-party models.

Alibaba reportedly supported the model’s training, though neither company commented.

Models including ChatGPT and Claude are unavailable in mainland China, making Apple’s strategy there different from its approach in other major markets for now.

The development follows Alibaba confirming its Apple partnership in February 2025. More recently, China’s internet regulator registered Apple Intelligence for use on iPhones.

Previous reporting said Alibaba’s Qwen model and technology from Baidu would be incorporated into the localized system.

Reuters says it remains unclear how Apple’s new model will work alongside those third-party models. Apple Intelligence is expected to reach China in the coming months following an iOS update, according to the report.

Elsewhere, Apple’s overhauled Siri AI is scheduled to launch publicly with iOS 27 this fall where available.

It will initially support select English variants, while iPhone and iPad availability in the EU is delayed. China’s timeline remains unconfirmed.

articles.title: Review: Acer's 6K Touchscreen Display Turns Your Mac Into a Giant iPad, Sort Of
articles.subtitle: Acer recently came out with a new 6K 31.5-inch display, the ProDesigner PE320QXT. It's a touchscreen display that's able to work with a Mac using touch drivers, and it's aimed at professional creators.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Acer recently came out with a new 6K 31.5-inch display, the ProDesigner PE320QXT. It's a touchscreen display that's able to work with a Mac using touch drivers, and it's aimed at professional creators. It's fun to use, but there are some compromises, and this is not the display to get unless you really want touch integration.

This is a big, heavy display. It's thicker than my Apple Studio Display, and it's thicker than any other display I've tested, likely because of the touch layer. It does have a tapered design so the sides aren't quite as thick as the middle, but this isn't a modern-looking monitor. It doesn't resemble something designed in 2026, especially with the button-based controls and the thick bezels.

If someone told me this was a display from 2006, I'd believe it. With its stand, the ProDesigner weighs about 22 pounds, and it takes up a lot of room on my desk.

The display uses an IPS panel and has a resolution of 6016 x 3384, and it can connect to a Mac using HDMI or USB-C. I tested it on a 16-inch M1 Max MacBook Pro running macOS Golden Gate and an M4 MacBook Air. By default, macOS uses a 3008 x 1692 scaled resolution, which is a good compromise between display quality and sizing. It can be set at higher resolutions, including the full 6016 x 3384, but window sizing and text get smaller as resolution goes up.

articles.title: Apple Arcade in September: Four new games added to the service again this month
articles.subtitle: Macworld Gaming subscription services are all the rage now, but Apple Arcade isn’t a little different from the likes of PlayStation Plus, EA Play, or Xbox Game Pass. If you’ve got questions about it, we’ve got plenty of answers.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Gaming subscription services are all the rage now, but Apple Arcade isn’t a little different from the likes of PlayStation Plus, EA Play, or Xbox Game Pass. If you’ve got questions about it, we’ve got plenty of answers.

Updated September 4, 2026: There are four new games on the service again this month: Art of Fauna: Cozy Puzzles+, Block Blast+, Coloring Games for Families+, and Let’s Play! Oink Games+.

What is Apple Arcade?

Apple Arcade is a gaming subscription service for iPhone, iPad, Mac, and AppleTV that features several hundred games. The games are a mix of genres and styles, and include original games you’ll only find on the service and others that can be found on the regular App Store or even other platforms. Apple Arcade isn’t a streaming service like Xbox Live Cloud Gaming or GeForce NOW. Games must be downloaded onto your device in order to be played.

What do I need to run it?

Apple Arcade was made available as part of iOS 13, iPad OS 13, tvOS 13, and macOS Catalina or later. Some of the more visually-intensive games may only run well on newer hardware, though, and some Mac games require macOS 11 (Big Sur).

How much does Apple Arcade cost?

Apple Arcade costs $6.99/£6.99 per month, and you’ll also get a one-month free trial or you can get three months free if you purchase a new iPhone, iPad, Apple TV or Mac. To claim your free trial click here.

You can get Apple Arcade for less than $6.99 a month if you subscribe for a year upfront. A year of Apple Arcade is $49.99/£49.99 (so $4.16 a month). If you’re currently on the $6.99 month-to-month plan and want to switch to the annual plan and save some money, you can do so on your iPhone or iPad. Open the App Store app, then tap your account icon in the upper right. Tap Subscriptions, then tap the entry for Apple Arcade. Here, you can switch to the annual plan.

Apple Arcade is also included in the Apple One subscription bundles, which range from $20 a month to $38 a month and include access to Apple Music and Apple TV and iCloud storage. There is also a month free trial of Apple One. To claim the trial, or sign up for Apple One, click here.

How do I sign up for Apple Arcade?

There isn’t an Apple Arcade app—it’s built into the App Store. On your iPhone, iPad, or Mac open the App Store and look for the Apple Arcade tab at the bottom of the screen (or in the left column on macOS). A sign-up screen with a Try It Free button will appear. After the trial you’ll be charged either the monthly or annual fee, depending on your selection.

When subscribing, you’ll need to enter your Apple ID password or use Touch ID or Face ID to sign in, and you’ll have to confirm your subscription purchase a few times.

Once you’re done with the sign up, the Arcade section of the App Store shows what games are available to you. To access a game, tap on it in the App Store, then tap the Get button. When the game is done installing on your device, the Get button turns into a Play button, and you can tap it to launch the game. The game app icon will also appear on your device’s Home page.

On the Apple TV, there actually is an Arcade app. Open that to see the sign-up offer. You’ll also find an Arcade tab within the App Store.

Does my subscription include family sharing?

Yes. One $6.99 per month subscription can be shared between up to six people (including you).

Apple started informing developers today that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now drop support for Intel-based Macs.

In the email, Apple says:

We’re reaching out to let you know that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now remove support for Intel-based Mac computers. By removing support for Intel-based Mac computers, you can simplify your development and optimize your download and on-device size. To remove Intel support, update your app build settings to “arm64” only. Then rebuild and submit your app to the Mac App Store.

By removing support for Intel-based Mac computers, you can simplify your development and optimize your download and on-device size.

To remove Intel support, update your app build settings to “arm64” only. Then rebuild and submit your app to the Mac App Store.

Previously, developers were required to offer Intel compatibility. With today’s change, developers can drop support for Intel-based Macs. Intel users, however, can continue using the last version of the app compatible with their machine.

The changes come as macOS 27 Golden Gate drops support for Intel-powered Macs altogether. Apple also announced last year that Rosetta 2, the software that translates Intel apps for Apple Silicon, will be discontinued after macOS 27 (with some exceptions for for certain games).

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

articles.subtitle: Company behind the iconic puzzle game responds to Trump administration's controversial arcade games The White House's penchant for using video games to peddle hate has largely been met with silence or inaction in the video game industry, even when it involves...
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Company behind the iconic puzzle game responds to Trump administration's controversial arcade games

The White House's penchant for using video games to peddle hate has largely been met with silence or inaction in the video game industry, even when it involves companies that are notoriously litigious about their intellectual property. Tetris, it seems, may be a rare exception to this disappointing trend.

On Thursday, the White House published a series of arcade games themed around the Trump administration's bigoted political agenda. Among other things, the games encouraged players to digitally build an immigration wall with Tetris blocks and arrest virtual people of color depicted crossing the border. Most of the games were simple knockoffs of classics like Flappy Bird and Snake. Marketing around the digital initiative made more blatant references to specific brands, such as the Nintendo GameCube logo.

Though the games aren't particularly good, they're extremely visible and hateful. More critically, the White House arcade games are potentially fertile ground for copyright infringement cases.

One day after White House social media accounts shared the games, the company behind Tetris issued a response. On Instagram, the Tetris account said that the brand believed "in the power of connection and bringing people together, not dividing them." A follow-up reply to the post, also authored by the brand, clarified that the company was not involved in the creation of the controversial game.

"We take copyright infringement very seriously," the Tetris Company added.

The company did not share what measures it would take to defend its copyright, and so far, Build the Wall is still publicly accessible. If the company does take action, it would be one of the first high-profile gaming companies, if not the only one, fighting back against the White House in a public way.

Trump uses video game imagery to trigger its base

In recent years, the Trump administration has made heavy use of video game branding on social media to advertise questionable political causes. Many major brands, from Halo to Pokémon, have been used by the White House in this way — but seemingly none of them sought legal action against the administration. At best, gaming companies have only distanced themselves from the White House's antics by clarifying that they had no involvement with the campaign.

Should Tetris actually pursue legal action through a copyright claim, the White House may need to pull Build the Wall down from its website. But considering how frequently the Trump administration ignores court orders and brushes off criticism from artists, there's little hope that the Tetris Company will effect change. For now, the company shared a message with all of its fans.

"To our fans everywhere: we love you, we see you, and we're grateful to have you in our community," the post reads.

Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API.

Muse Voice Transcribe powers system-wide dictation on Mac

Meta Superintelligence Labs says Muse Voice Transcribe combines streaming automatic speech recognition with speaker diarization and endpointing.

In practical terms, it can transcribe speech as it happens, separate speakers across recordings with 20-plus voices, and determine when someone has finished talking, all without a separate post-processing step.

The model was trained across more than 70 languages, with 25 validated at launch. It supports audio longer than an hour, plus native code-switching within or between sentences. Language, keyword, and context biasing can further improve recognition.

Rather than using one fixed tradeoff between speed and accuracy, Muse Voice Transcribe decides how long to listen before committing each word. Meta calls this “adaptive delay.” The system can move quickly through easier speech while using more audio context for difficult words.

Meta says the model ranks first on the Artificial Analysis streaming speech-to-text leaderboard as of September 1.

Muse Voice Transcribe is available today through the Meta Model API for $3 per 1,000 audio-minutes, equivalent to $0.18 per hour.

It is also already powering dictation in Meta AI for Mac and Muse Code. On Mac, users can hold the Fn key to dictate into any application.

articles.title: After Conquering Esports, T1 Faker Officially Stuns the TCG Market With a $50K Card
articles.subtitle: Riftbound resellers are asking for — and getting — ridiculous returns on a $360 set Riot Games' Riftbound is making a big splash on the TCG market this week, thanks to a new release that quickly sold out and is going for nearly 20 times its asking price...
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Riftbound resellers are asking for — and getting — ridiculous returns on a $360 set

Riot Games' Riftbound is making a big splash on the TCG market this week, thanks to a new release that quickly sold out and is going for nearly 20 times its asking price on the secondhand market. The Riftbound x T1 2025 Worlds Champion Signature Edition started shipping out to buyers over the past week, and many have since quickly been flipped on eBay, with some auctions fetching upward of $7,000.

Many of the sets sold on eBay have been going for $5,000 to $6,000, but some resellers are aiming much, much higher, particularly when it comes to a serial-numbered card in the Riftbound bundle "signed" by T1 player Faker. Multiple sellers are asking $50,000 for the card.

What's in the Riftbound x T1 2025 Worlds Champion Signature Edition set?

Riot's Riftbound x T1 2025 Worlds Champion Signature Edition bundle is inspired by T1's win at Worlds 2025 and features five League of Legends Champions on cards with new artwork and a unique card frame. Each card was selected by a T1 member of the winning team, Riot says. The cards in the limited-edition bundle are gold-foiled and serialized, and one card in each set is randomly gold-stamped with that player’s signature.

The cards included in the Riftbound x T1 2025 Worlds Champion Signature Edition set are: Ambessa, The Wolf (Doran); Galio, Indefatigable (Faker); Miss Fortune, Buccaneer (Gumayusi); Seraphine, Not Alone (Keria); and Xin Zhao, Vigilant (Oner). Unsurprisingly, T1's most popular and highest-earning player, Faker (real name Sang Hyeok Lee), is commanding the biggest prices on the secondhand market.

Multiple sellers are trying to resell bundles that feature Faker's gold-stamped signature for tens of thousands of dollars.

Incidentally, the standard version of the Galio, Indefatigable Riftbound card goes for around $0.26, according to TCGPlayer.

According to Riot, only 10,125 versions of the Riftbound x T1 2025 Worlds Champion Signature Edition set were produced in English. With a one-in-five chance at getting a gold-stamped Faker card, that means just 2,025 of the sets will include his signature. While it doesn't appear that anyone's biting yet on dropping $50,000 (or even $30,000) on a Faker-signed Riftbound card, the highest-end auctions have plenty of watchers gawking to see what sells and for how much.

Over the past year, some Riftbound cards have sold for prices as high as $39,000.

Riot Games officially launched Riftbound in October 2025, with a series of decks and booster boxes. Riot quickly faced the same issue that The Pokémon Company did, with sets selling out and quickly being scalped by speculators. For the Riftbound x T1 2025 Worlds Champion Signature Edition bundle, Riot attempted to curb bots and resellers by requiring a Riot ID and limiting sets to one purchase per print run.

Even still, with limited numbers come buyers hoping to capitalize on rarity, and it appears that some scalpers are profiting handsomely.

We'll keep an eye on how well the Riftbound x T1 2025 Worlds Champion Signature Edition bundle sells after the hype dies down a bit.

We’ve also had the chance to see many of these features in action through the beta, with the full release now likely to be only days away.

Golden Gate continues Apple’s tradition of naming macOS releases after iconic Californian landmarks. macOS 27 will support all Macs powered by Apple silicon, marking the end of the road for Intel-based Macs. While Intel models won’t be eligible for the new operating system, Apple is expected to continue providing security updates for them for some time.

Apple

Siri AI: A redesigned conversational Siri that can answer questions, understand personal and onscreen context, access the web and take actions across apps.

Apple Intelligence: Systemwide proofreading, smarter writing tools, improved dictation and automatic file and folder naming.

Safari upgrades: Automatic tab grouping, webpage change alerts with Notify Me, AI-generated extensions and faster, more efficient browsing.

Smarter Messages and Mail: Personalized Smart Reply, better search and syncing, contextual suggestions and improved reliability.

articles.title: Me: You can now run DLSS 5 on AMD GPUs. My RX 9070 XT: Please stop, it hurts us
articles.subtitle: A new app allows you to inject DLSS Neural Rendering deep into games even if you're running an AMD card. You probably won't want to, though.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Another day, another DLSS 5 story that actually kinda doesn't involve Nvidia itself doing anything, because it seems now AMD GPU owners can get in on the act. A new homebrew app has been released on Github that will allow you to run the DLSS Neural Rendering feature on a Radeon GPU. I've tried it and it works, but damn does it hurt the poor Radeon silicon.

From having DLSS 5.dll files plucked from an early access version of NBA 2K27, we've had modders working hard to create surprisingly polished ways to essentially get the tech working in practically any game, even if it doesn't natively support traditional DLSS itself.

I've been playing around with it a lot this past week, even to the point of jamming it into Football Manager 26 just to see what would happen. And, y'know what, I kinda like the result so I'm keeping it. I wasn't expecting that, and I also wasn't expecting this technology, created by Nvidia, to appear so quickly on AMD GPUs.

Historically we've found that where Nvidia goes, so AMD follows, at least in the GPU feature space, but it seems like AMD might not actually have to do much this time. Well, apart from actually make the silicon a little more tensor-friendly.

Because I have spent the afternoon trying to get the new app from user danielblnc on Github to work on my Radeon RX 9070 XT in Cyberpunk 2077. Essentially you download the DLSS-NR-on-AMD file, drop it into the relevant folder (the bin/x64 folder in the Cyberpunk 2077 directory in Steam, for example) and run it. So long as you have the necessary nvngx_dlssnr.dll file that's been doing the rounds installed in the same place it ought to work.

It didn't.

Initially Windows flagged it as containing a virus, but I did some checking around with VirusTotal and seemingly the Defender flag is a machine learning false positive. Probably. But even then I still struggled to have it running happily.

I am not entirely sure what I did wrong, but when I enabled the feature in-game all I got was a black output where the 3D world ought to be, even though the HUD and game kept on running. After some file deletion, redownloading, verifying of integrity (mine and Cyberpunk's), and a rollback of my AMD Adrenalin drivers, I finally got it working. Kinda. I mean it's still kinda crashy, and I can only now launch Cyberpunk 2077 directly from the.exe file rather than from Steam, but it works.

But my poor GPU wished I hadn't. Now, we know that DLSS 5 is a hell of a resource hog on an RTX 50-series GPU that it's designed for, with a touted 50 - 60% performance hit officially noted by Nvidia, so I should have known it would trouble the AMD GPU.

DLSS NR on Nvidia

DLSS 5 was designed for GeForce GPUs, so is a little more capable, but still a massive resource hog.

Still… running at 4K RT Ultra settings is tough enough, and I was getting just 61 fps on the RX 9070 XT even with FSR 4 set to Balanced. And then flicking the DLSS Neural Rendering toggle to 'on' made that figure drop to just 9 fps.

And I thought the 73% drop Andy found with NBA 2K27 was rough.

DLSS NR on AMD

AMD GPUs running DLSS 5 looks great, but runs horribly.

Now it's worth noting that the fact it is running at all on AMD GPUs is impressive on its own, but it's not going to make any Radeon graphics card owners any happier about it when they're getting unplayable frame rates out of their new ill-gotten pretties. An 85% performance drop is not sustainable. Nice for screenshots though, eh?

The issue is that AMD's RDNA 4 doesn't have the level of dedicated silicon for the sort of matrix calculations the feature is running… in the same way that RTX 20-series chips don't.

The Turing architecture does have Tensor Cores, but they're far weaker compared to those in the RTX 40- or RTX 50-series, and the shared resources AMD plucks from the standard RDNA 4 Compute Units for these sorts of calculations aren't as robust either. Hence the weaker performance.

articles.title: Perplexity Introduces ‘Hybrid Compute’ for Computer Agent on Apple Silicon Macs
articles.subtitle: Source: Perplexity. Perplexity has announced hybrid compute for Personal Computer on Apple silicon Macs. Personal Computer already combined cloud-based Computer tasks with access to local files and apps, but its AI processing was primarily cloud-based.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Perplexity has announced hybrid compute for Personal Computer on Apple silicon Macs. Personal Computer already combined cloud-based Computer tasks with access to local files and apps, but its AI processing was primarily cloud-based. Recently, Perplexity also introduced Portable Computer, a local-first version of Computer that can escalate work to the cloud with a user’s permission.

Hybrid compute approaches the problem from a different direction. Tasks start in the cloud but if a new local classifier detects potentially sensitive information, the user is alerted and asked whether they want to route it to a local model, although users also have the option to let the flagged data be used by a frontier cloud-based model. Gemma E4B, Qwen3.6 35B-A3B, and a Perplexity post-trained version of Qwen3.6 35B are available at launch for that local work, with more models to come in the future.

Tasks that don’t require sensitive information are handled in the cloud by frontier models that also orchestrate the cloud and local tasks. Users select the cloud orchestrator and Perplexity chooses the helper frontier models used.

Another key feature is that hybrid compute works with tasks begun from an iPhone or iPad, too. Those devices could already kick off a session, but now they can also run tasks that use sensitive information locally if your Mac is turned on and running Perplexity.

Yesterday, I got a demo of the feature that walked through three scenarios:

an attorney researching a legal brief, with sensitive client data on their Mac, allowing them to update it locally,

an analyst using web-based data to update a confidential slide deck for a presentation about a company’s financials, and

a small business owner kicking off pricing research from her iPhone that was combined with private pricing data for her business that never left her Mac.

I haven’t tried hybrid compute myself yet, but if it works as advertised, it’s a big step forward for Perplexity, and one that a lot of its competitors are also chasing. AI agents are only as good as the tools and data to which they have access.

Tool calling has been a big focus over the last year and more, but data privacy is an equally important issue that needs to be solved before more companies, especially those in regulated industries, adopt agentic tools like Personal Computer. It’s good to see Perplexity tackling this head-on.

articles.title: Siri will sometimes summarize webpages and videos from within Safari and YouTube apps
articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.title: You Can Get 5 Excellent 90+ Rated Steam Games For Under $25 Right Now
articles.subtitle: There’s a holiday weekend ahead. Need something good to play? Here are five games that are all excellent and also wildly cheap right now on Steam.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
There’s a holiday weekend ahead. Need something good to play? Here are five games that are all excellent and also wildly cheap right now on Steam.

Tomb Raider (2013)

What if Uncharted was more like a Metroidvania? That’s one of the questions asked in the first game that kicked off the modern Tomb Raider revival. It’s got great bow-and-arrow action and a good story, and it’s currently only $3 on Steam. Or you can get the whole Survivor trilogy for just under $11 (until September 7).

From the Kotaku review:

You can feel the ambitions of the Crystal Dynamics creative team in the design of the game’s component parts. The presentational elements—plot, dialogue, voice acting and art design—all shine. Some characters lean too heavily on type but not so much as to be really annoying. This is a beautiful game to look at, too, with great animations and modeling/texture work that’s bursting with vivid, horrid detail in the characters and environments.

Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun

Atmospheric strategy and great level design set in Japan’s Edo period. That’s what’s on offer in Shadow Tactics, a strategy game that led a revival in real-time isometric stealth gameplay. Normally $40, it’s currently just $4 to own on Steam.

From the Kotaku review:

What keeps me poring over every map though, more than even the strategies and planning involved, is how pretty everything looks. There’s a wonderful toy-like quality to the game’s world, like it’s a giant diorama made by master craftsmen, and it’s a pleasure finding downtime to just pan the camera around and take everything in, from the gentle flowing of a river to the busywork of townspeople to the chaos of a battle unfolding around the map’s edges.

Grim Dawn

It’s not Warhammer, it’s Grim Dawn. Considered a spiritual successor to Diablo 2 when it was released a decade ago, the action-RPG takes isometric looting to a unique, Victorian-inspired apocalyptic fantasy world. It was always lauded as more hardcore than the pure sugar rush of some loot-based Diablo -likes, but recent updates have steered it more in the direction of a top-down Soulslike, to the chagrin of some long-time fans. For others, that’s a plus.

If you’ve never dipped your toes in this pond before, you can currently do so for just $3.75 on Steam. No Kotaku review of this one, so you’ll have to trust the 94-percent positive rating from users on Steam.

A Plague Tale: Innocence

A Plague Tale: Innocence holds up as a beautiful and haunting stealth adventure. There are shades of The Last of Us here, reflected through the lens of a rat-infested 1300s Europe. It’s sort of like an 8-to-10-hour playable movie, but a very good one. You can give it a shot for just $4 on Steam right now, and it’s the perfect follow-up if you recently played the action-oriented prequel, Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy, without having already experienced the rest of the series.

From a spoiler-filled Kotaku write-up:

It’s been so long since a game has truly scared me that A Plague Tale: Innocence caught me completely off guard. Tense, terrifying, and meticulously crafted, Plague Tale excels at making you feel utterly helpless. Set in late 1349 in Aquitaine, France, the medieval setting is one of the game’s strengths, distinguishing itself with the backdrop of a dark, and tragic, history.

Guardians of the Galaxy

Five years later, it still doesn’t feel like Guardians of the Galaxy has gotten its due. Hurt by the mess around the live-service Avengers game as well as broader burnout with the MCU, the game failed to find the audience it deserved, and not enough people experienced one of the best linear comic-book video games of the modern era.

articles.title: The 14 Best at Gamescom 2026
articles.subtitle: Get these on your wishlist ASAP Gamescom 2026 was full of surprises, from reveals of never-seen-before games during Opening Night Live to the announcement of a remaster for one of the best games of all time.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Get these on your wishlist ASAP

Gamescom 2026 was full of surprises, from reveals of never-seen-before games during Opening Night Live to the announcement of a remaster for one of the best games of all time. Beyond the opening showcase, though, Gamescom is also a trade show and consumer gaming event — basically, the replacement for E3 — held in a sprawling convention hall with hundreds of games to play.

Polygon was on the floor this year, and while there, we went hands-on with a ton of those games, from AAA behemoths like Fable to under-the-radar indies like Wilderings: The Lost Spring.

But what were the absolute best games we played while we were out in Cologne, Germany? Here's our list of the top 14 games we played at Gamescom 2026, in no particular order.

1 Fable

We'd be remiss not to start with one of the most anticipated AAA releases of the whole event, right? You can read more about Fable in our dedicated preview, but the gist of it is as follows: tight, satisfying combat with fluid mechanics that allow you to switch between melee, ranged, and magic with ease.

Our fighting-focused demo involved following the very British Humphry (voiced by comedian Matt King, of Super Hans fame from Peep Show ) through an old mine, where undead foes arose around every corner. It then culminated in a fantastic boss battle against a ferocious spirit in a misty bog, and even though Fable is going to be a shorter game than we were expecting, I cannot wait to play more. — Ford James

The new Fable lets players fully embrace a power fantasy

2 Worms Galactic Tactics

Tactics games are on a comeback right now, and Worms Galactic Tactics is trying something much-needed for the genre: to make it even more accessible. Even though tactics games are fairly simple in comparison to other strategy sub-genres (anyone who can get their head around a 4X game is a wizard in my book), they do have somewhat of a learning curve.

With Worms Galactic Tactics, it's implementing roguelite mechanics and treating it as, essentially, another Worms game. The only difference is this time, the playing field is 3D. I only had a quick blast on the demo but this may be the best take on the turn-based Worms formula yet. — Ford James

3 Alien Deathstorm

Alien Deathstorm is one of the most video-gamey video games I've played in a long time. There are a lot of aliens, a devastating storm, and death like you wouldn't believe. The 20-minute demo stuck me in a late-game mission where I needed to repair a reactor, and the sandbox nature of the level meant there were multiple paths to achieve this.

Do I investigate the control room, the core, the substation, or somewhere else entirely? Each location had different leads and problems to be solved, but I was also being stalked by aliens, with only an SMG to defend myself. Oh, and the aliens react to your behavior: go in guns blazing and you're gonna attract a hell of a lot more. This is one to watch for 2027. — Ford James

4 Exodus

For four years, Exodus has been heralded as the second coming of Mass Effect. It's looked the part the entire time. And now that I've gone hands-on with it, yes, by every measure, it holds up to that lofty comparison.

The narrative RPG features third-person combat in a space-based sci-fi setting, but also features no shortage of complex skill trees, interesting party members (who you can date), an impactful morality system, ancient alien relics, and an interstellar mystery that could affect all of humanity. — Ari Notis

articles.title: Apple to Mac developers: It’s time to let go of Intel
articles.subtitle: Macworld When Apple introduced its M-series chips, it also marked the beginning of the end for software written for Intel Macs. It’s been nearly six years since then, and Apple has let developers know that they can bring Intel Mac development to a close.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
When Apple introduced its M-series chips, it also marked the beginning of the end for software written for Intel Macs. It’s been nearly six years since then, and Apple has let developers know that they can bring Intel Mac development to a close.

In an email to developers, Apple said:

We’re reaching out to let you know that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now remove support for Intel-based Mac computers. By removing support for Intel-based Mac computers, you can simplify your development and optimize your download and on-device size.

We’re reaching out to let you know that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now remove support for Intel-based Mac computers.

By removing support for Intel-based Mac computers, you can simplify your development and optimize your download and on-device size.

When Apple announced macOS 26 Tahoe last year, the company said it would be the last version to support Intel Macs. This new announcement takes another step toward dropping Intel altogether. A new Apple support document adds this vital bit of information:

macOS 27: Final release to support Rosetta — Intel-only apps will no longer run on Mac computers with Apple silicon after this update.

Now it’s up to developers to determine when to stop with Intel code. App designers will need to determine how many of their users still use Intel Macs before they can drop development, which means that some will need to continue to support Intel for a while. If you use an Intel app, reach out to the app developer to find out their plans.

During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

articles.title: PAX Is Officially Coming to the 'Dork Population' Capital of Texas With New Tabletop Show
articles.subtitle: PAX is going back south with a new Unplugged show For the first time in approximately six years, PAX is heading to the southern U.S. for an exciting new event.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
PAX is going back south with a new Unplugged show

For the first time in approximately six years, PAX is heading to the southern U.S. for an exciting new event. PAX Unplugged Houston, the latest iteration of the tabletop gaming convention from Penny Arcade, co-organized by ReedPop, will host its inaugural show at the George R. Brown Convention Center in Houston on June 25–27, 2027.

In 1998, Jerry Holkins and Mike Krahulik created Penny Arcade, a webcomic based on their experiences and passion for video games and the gaming industry. In 2004, the two authors decided the world (or more accurately, the U.S. West Coast) needed a convention dedicated exclusively to gaming. And so, Penny Arcade Expo was born, later rebranded as PAX.

“I remember the very first PAX, when we had like 1,300 people in attendance,” Mike Krahulik said in a video interview with Polygon. “And Jerry and I were sitting and this guy comes up to us and says, ‘I didn’t have a very good time. ’ And Jerry and I felt horrible. And we still feel that way. There's no reason we should feel personally responsible for this show anymore!

But if I see somebody who isn’t having a good time, I still feel bad. I think it’s important to have two people who feel a responsibility that you have a good time at their party. ”

This feeling of personal responsibility and community service served as the strong foundation on which PAX expanded to four, now five, yearly events. Its longevity owes a lot to Holkins and Krahulik remaining true to their roots for more than 20 years.

Among all the shows, PAX Unplugged has a different energy, according to Holkins. “I always feel so energized after it that I immediately want to do another one.”

“And that’s the point of the country where we don’t have a PAX,” Krahulik added. “The weak point, where we need to strike for maximum damage.”

The organizers chose Houston based on infrastructure capacity, airport size, hotel availability, and favorable demographics, including a large, young, tech-savvy population. “We think the dork population is quite high in Houston,” Krahulik said.

PAX Unplugged is an expression of the growth of tabletop games

This won’t be PAX’s first foray into the South. PAX South was held in San Antonio from 2015 to 2020, but the event was canceled in 2021. The organizers believe now is the best time for a comeback, and for a second yearly Unplugged. The tabletop industry is experiencing a period of massive growth and creative flourishing, and the Penny Arcade team is well aware.

“We've always used PAX as a tool to expose video gamers to tabletop stuff,” Holkins said. “As tabletop has gotten more powerful, sophisticated, and interesting, obviously PAX Unplugged was the truest expression of what we can do there. But if you go take a look at PAX East, a whole third of the show’s floor is just tabletop stuff. There's always been this secret tabletop con at PAX shows.”

“Very early on, we decided that was going to be a part of the show,” Krahulik added. “We wanted to tell people, ‘Hey, what you like isn't necessarily video games. What you like is cool systems, interesting rules and mechanics. And you can get that in lots of different places.’ I had never played Dungeons & Dragons before Acquisitions Incorporated; that was the same idea, showing video game players that these tabletop games are just as cool.”

Acquisitions Incorporated, or Acq. Inc. for longtime fans, was a pioneer in the D&D actual play show field. It started in 2008 as a podcast in partnership with Wizards of the Coast, and it has since evolved into live games held during the PAX conventions, several pre-recorded miniseries, and even an official Acquisitions Incorporated sourcebook for D&D 5th edition.

Daggerheart is now a PAX Unplugged mainstay

At PAX Unplugged 2025, it was revealed that, after almost two decades of loyal service to D&D, Acquisitions Incorporated was switching to Daggerheart, the TTRPG created by Critical Role. The announcement shocked the tabletop world; or at least, it should have. Polygon was one of the few outlets reporting on it.

“We don’t understand it either,” Holkins said, jokingly, of the lack of buzz around the change. “We started it a long time ago, and all we've tried to do is just show how much fun it can be to play these games with your friends. But when I was a kid, I got in incredible trouble for playing D&D, and I couldn't have those types of books in the house.

So I started exploring the other RPGs out there, alternative systems. Some are better at different things, and some expose different angles on the same stuff. The D&D system lets you do a little bit of everything because everybody knows it so well that the system itself sort of fades into the background.

articles.title: The Potential of M6 and M5 Ultra for Local AI on macOS
articles.subtitle: Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio. You can read more details about the announcement and related specs in John’s overview.

As someone who’s been working with an M3 Ultra Mac Studio (on loan from Apple) with 512 GB of RAM for the past year (plus two separate M4 Mac minis) with a particular focus on local AI models and performance gains enabled by Apple’s MLX framework, I obviously am very interested in these new machines.

To give you some context: my current workspace for my upcoming iOS and iPadOS 27 review, which lives in Notion, is entirely managed by a series of local agents running the latest DeepSeek-V4-Flash via MLX on the Mac Studio, which continuously scan the project for new notes, sources, and research material that is automatically categorized and linked in the chapters that I’m writing.

So, yes, I’m sure I’ll have more thoughts on the new Mac minis and Mac Studios soon. In the meantime, I thought it’d be fun to break down the local AI-related details from Apple.

First, the M6. While it may not be the powerhouse that the M5 Ultra is, it’s an interesting new chip because of its new 2 nm process and dual Neural Engine system:

M6 is built using cutting-edge 2 nm process technology, packing greater transistor density into a smaller die for a major leap in performance and power efficiency. M6 also introduces a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, providing up to 2x the peak compute over previous generations to make on-device AI workflows run even faster. System frameworks can automatically utilize both engines simultaneously, enabling applications to see faster model execution.

But that’s not all: the new 12-core GPU (which has two more cores than the M4’s old GPU) now features Neural Accelerators in each core for the first time on the Mac mini. The result, according to Apple, is “4x faster AI performance and 2x faster graphics than Mac mini with M4”. If these numbers hold up and scale linearly, a local Mixture-of-Experts model such as Qwen 3.

5-35B-A3B, which would run at ~17 tokens/sec on average on a base M4 Mac mini with 16 GB of RAM, could realistically generate output at over 60 tokens/second with the base model M6 Mac mini.

Based on what we’ve seen so far, the one downside of the M6 Mac mini is that it does not have Thunderbolt 5 ports; those are exclusive to the M5 Pro model, also announced today. As Apple also notes, Thunderbolt 5 allows multiple M5 Pro Mac minis to run local AI models as a single cluster (for example, using something like exo ).

Alas, that won’t be possible with the M6 Mac mini and its Thunderbolt 4 bandwidth bottleneck. Nonetheless, I’d be intrigued to compare the performance of the widely regarded Qwen3. 8-27B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash models on the new M6 Mac mini.

Moving on to the flagship M5 Ultra Mac Studio, let’s start here:

With M5 Ultra, Mac Studio achieves up to 4.3x the peak AI compute performance of M3 Ultra and a staggering 9.8x more than M1 Ultra. Combined with up to 512GB of unified memory and 1.2TB/s of memory bandwidth, 50 percent higher than before, Mac Studio lets users run massive models entirely on device with complete privacy — without counting tokens or worrying about rising cloud costs.

As seen on the Mac Studio’s product page, the 512 GB RAM version of the M5 Ultra Mac Studio will only be available in “late October”. Unlike the M6, the M5 Ultra supports Thunderbolt 5, which will allow customers to run multiple Mac Studios in a cluster with shared memory to distribute inference across machines. And, according to Apple, a cluster of four Mac Studios yields three times the performance of a single Mac Studio.

Speaking from personal experience, I know that my M3 Ultra Mac Studio using oMLX can run DeepSeek-V4-Flash locally with generation averaging 35 tokens/second. Assuming a linear 4x increase, that would put the same model at over 120 tokens/second on an M5 Ultra Mac Studio.

To put things in perspective, that kind of performance would be faster than any AI chatbot website, it’d be faster than many providers who offer a “fast” mode for their models, and it’d only be second to either dedicated NVIDIA PC clusters at home or specialized inference providers such as Cerebras or Groq …which are running in full-blown data centers.

Sure, you would need a computer that is likely going to cost more than $20,000 to make it happen, but it’d still be possible on a single machine that is small, quiet, and that – in theory – any consumer can buy off the shelf.

It’s also interesting to consider the implications of M5 Ultra for running much larger models that would have typically required aggressive quantization to even stay in memory and produce any useful output. For example, Z. ai’s GLM-5.

2 (a 744B MoE model) could run at up to 17 tokens/second on an M3 Ultra Mac Studio with 512 GB of RAM; the same person was even able to get the massive Kimi K3 model to run on a single machine…with decoding performance up to 3 tokens/second.

articles.title: Diagnosing sentiment in my typo-reporting workflow
articles.subtitle: This is more of a comment than a question. A few months ago I added a “Report a Typo” feature to Six Colors. The goal was to give people a simple place to go — sixcolors.com/typo …
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
A few months ago I added a “Report a Typo” feature to Six Colors. The goal was to give people a simple place to go — sixcolors.com/typo — if they found a mistake on the website. That Google form inserts the information into a Google Sheet, and a script attached to the Google Sheet kicks off a simple automation that sends me a notification in a couple different places.

This works pretty well. I’m using a very simple Google Apps script to fire off a webhook when there’s a new form submission. The webhook is running on Make.com, which we use for a bunch of simple web automations, but that’s an implementation detail. Make.com posts an item in a private Discord channel and also crafts a custom push notification to my phone using Pushover.

However, the moment I turned this feature on, I discovered the problem with asking people to report errors or typos: Some people see any open channel of communication as an open channel for any sort of communication. I immediately started getting more “this is more a comment than a question” items about articles than actual typo submissions. Commentary included personal preferences for writing style, web design, political references (real or imagined), and much more.

I’m going to make an admission: This sort of feedback is maddening. I want to be alerted about mistakes on the site so I can fix them promptly, but I am not interested in receiving push notifications regarding your opinion of the professionalism and appropriateness of my writing style.

Unfortunately, it’s an open form. There’s nothing to be done. Or is there?

This is a challenge that can’t really be solved by looking for a bunch of keywords. You need wholesale sentiment analysis of the entire submission. This is—brace yourself—actually a good use of a large language model.

I solved this problem by using a plug-in within Make.com that lets me get a reply back from a cloud LLM that uses a simple model with an API cost of pennies per use, but you could also just use Shortcuts to build a version of this automation that runs on a Mac (Tahoe or Golden Gate) using Apple’s built-in models. It works just fine in Shortcuts on my Mac, via the Use Model action. (See screenshot above.)

Here’s the prompt I’m currently using:

Your task is binary classification. Input: a user-submitted comment about an article, claiming to report an error. Output: one token only: ALLOW or REJECT. Definition of ALLOW: A concrete, objective, verifiable issue in the article.

articles.title: Apple Announces New M6 and M5 Pro Mac minis, Along with M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studios
articles.subtitle: Source: Apple. Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.

The headline feature of the M6 chip is that it’s Apple’s first 2-nanometer chip. The chip also includes “a larger 12-core CPU complex with the world’s fastest CPU core, a larger 12-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and up to 170GB/s of unified memory bandwidth.”

Looking more closely at the M6, Apple says it consists of two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores and is 1.2x faster in multithreaded performance than an M5 and up to 2.4x faster than an M1. Apple says the GPU delivers nearly 30% more peak GPU compute for AI than the M5. The M6’s 10% faster memory bandwidth will help with AI tasks, too, but its 32GB memory ceiling will limit which models can run locally.

The M6 mini’s GPU sounds impressive, too, with two more cores, Neural Accelerators for each core, which is a first for the mini. According to Apple, that leads to an up to four-fold increase in AI performance and a 2x graphics bump compared to the M4 mini. The Neural Engine has also been improved.

Apple also introduced an M5 Pro mini. It’s understandable if you find it confusing that the base model Mac mini has a more recent generation chipset than the more expensive model. What matters more than the chip generation is the “Pro” in M5 Pro, which makes it more capable than the M6, which has been designed for entry-level models.

The same sort of asymmetry occurred with the 2025 Mac Studio, which included an M4 Max model alongside the M3 Ultra. A big part of that difference is the M5 Pro mini’s support for 64GB of memory (double the M6 version’s top memory spec) and its 307GB/s of memory bandwidth compared to the M6 model’s 170GB/s memory bandwidth.

As for the M5 Ultra, which debuts in the Mac Studio, it sounds like a beast. According to Apple, the chip uses a next-generation version of its UltraFusion technology, resulting in a quad-die architecture for the first time in an Apple silicon chip. In addition, the M5 Ultra features an “up-to-36-core CPU and up-to-80-core GPU with a massive 1.2TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, 50 percent more than M3 Ultra.”

Here’s what Sri Santhanam, Apple’s vice president of Silicon Engineering Group, had to say about the new chips:

Today, we’re debuting the next giant leap in performance and AI compute for Apple silicon with the incredibly advanced M6 and the most powerful M-series chip yet, M5 Ultra. Built using the cutting-edge 2 nm process, M6 combines a new CPU complex, two additional CPU and GPU cores, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and more unified memory bandwidth to power through workloads with amazing energy efficiency.

And for the ultimate desktop performance and the ability to run massive AI models, M5 Ultra features a massive GPU, now with Neural Accelerators, and more unified memory bandwidth, pushing the boundaries of what a desktop can do.

Apple is fusing two dual-die M5 Max chips to create a single quad-die architecture. Apple says the M5 Ultra is “up to 1.25x higher single-threaded performance and up to 1.3x higher multithreaded performance than M3 Ultra”, the fastest Mac previously for sale. The M5 Ultra also supports up to an 80-core GPU with up to 4.5x the peak GPU compute for AI tasks compared to the M3 Ultra and features an upgraded Media Engine, according to Apple.

For those who don’t need the bleeding-edge performance of the M5 Ultra, Apple also introduced what sounds like a very capable M5 Max Mac Studio. The M5 Max version of the computer “features an 18-core CPU, an up-to-40-core GPU with Neural Accelerators built into each core, and up to 128GB of unified memory, accelerating complex pro and AI workloads.”

Macs featuring the new chips won’t be available immediately. You can preorder both online today for delivery on September 22 with the caveat that the M5 Ultra Mac Studio with 512GB of memory won’t be available until later in October.

Prices have risen too. The Mac mini models are both $100 more than the models they replace, while the M5 Ultra Mac Studio’s base configuration has risen $200. However, the M5 Max Mac Studio’s starting price hasn’t changed.

The Mac mini has been a lot of things to a lot of people over the years. From a compact, minimalist desktop system to a headless server, the mini is Apple’s jack-of-all-trades. More recently, demand for the tiny computer has surged as people put them to work for a variety of AI tasks, including running LLMs locally and serving as standalone Hermes and OpenClaw machines.

With memory and storage constraints, it’s no surprise that the base prices of the mini have risen. Despite those challenges, I hope Apple is able to produce enough to meet demand. I’ve loved having an M4 Pro model working away day and night in the background. It’s fast, relatively cool, energy efficient, and easy to run remotely.

If the claims of Apple’s press release hold up under real-world use, I expect the new models will be the same, but faster and more capable, which is especially important for tasks like running models locally.

I’m also looking forward to seeing how the new Mac Studios perform in real world tests. I’ve used an M1 Max Mac Studio for a few years now and it’s been every bit the workhorse computer I need for my day-to-day work. However, it’s beginning to show its age when it comes to AI tasks, coding, and other tasks. It may finally be time for me to upgrade.

articles.title: Siri demos in keynote were a little slow, but that’s good-ish news
articles.subtitle: A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.

articles.title: Steam Users Can Play This Chaotic Among Us-like for Free Until Sept. 7
articles.subtitle: Round up your friends, board a luxury space cruise and prepare to discover which one of you absolutely cannot be trusted Few things are better than getting a group of friends together online for some multiplayer chaos, and we're in a golden age for party...
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Round up your friends, board a luxury space cruise and prepare to discover which one of you absolutely cannot be trusted

Few things are better than getting a group of friends together online for some multiplayer chaos, and we're in a golden age for party gaming.

Among Us has basically reached legend status at this point. Then you've got games like Peak and REPO, which are guaranteed to turn a night of gaming with friends into a good time — assuming everyone survives and isn't sabotaging the crew. And right now, Meccha Chameleon is the latest hot indie game giving players another excuse to get a group together and cause some chaos.

But there are so many party games out there beyond the ones that manage to dominate Steam charts and social media feeds. Some fly a little under the radar, despite offering exactly the kind of ridiculous multiplayer fun that makes these games so easy to love. One of them is about to give you a particularly good excuse to round up your friends, because it's going free-to-play for the entire weekend.

That game is First Class Trouble, an indie party game from Invisible Walls that mixes cooperation, deception, and plenty of opportunities for things to go horribly wrong. And if you're looking for something new to play with friends this weekend, it's free to try on Steam right now.

What is First Class Trouble about?

First Class Trouble takes place aboard a luxurious intergalactic cruise ship where a group of passengers are trying to survive a disaster — and figure out which of their fellow travelers can't be trusted. Players take on the role of either Residents or Personoids, with both sides having very different ideas about how the voyage should end. The result is a social-deduction game where cooperation is essential, but trusting the wrong person can quickly turn a relaxing cruise into a complete disaster.

Players have to explore the ship, complete objectives and collect information while keeping an eye on everyone around them. Residents need to work together to identify the Personoids hiding among them, while the Personoids can lie, sabotage, and quietly eliminate anyone getting too close to the truth. Proximity voice chat adds another layer of paranoia, letting you whisper plans to your allies or make your case when someone inevitably accuses you of being a traitor.

You can play with between four and 12 players in custom games, making First Class Trouble an easy one to throw into the rotation when you've got a bigger group looking for something new.

And there's no better time to see whether your friends are actually trustworthy than this weekend. First Class Trouble is free to play on Steam through Sept. 6.

articles.title: App Report: AI to the rescue! No… really
articles.subtitle: Artificial Intelligence takes center stage in a few of the apps enjoying this week’s spotlight — and not the kind of AI that’s going to have you rolling your eyes or organizing a protest march against the nearest data center.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Artificial Intelligence takes center stage in a few of the apps enjoying this week’s spotlight — and not the kind of AI that’s going to have you rolling your eyes or organizing a protest march against the nearest data center. No, these are actually useful AI features that take some of the busy work of daily life out of your hands so you can concentrate on other things.

AI or no, we’re always looking for top macOS and iOS apps to feature here. If you’ve got something that fits that description, drop us a line at apps@sixcolors.com with a brief outline of the whats, whys, and wherefores.

Now on to this week’s selection…

Sortio

The folders on my Mac are a mess, but who has the time to make sure that everything is filed away in its proper place? AI does, according to the makers of Sortio, a macOS utility that promises to do the hard work of organization on your behalf.

Sortio taps into AI to look at file names and metadata to help it figure out where to put each file. You can also opt to let the utility read the file, sending a 4KB excerpt to your AI provider of choice for even more detailed sorting. (Sortio also offers an offline mode that uses Ollama or LM Studio to keep its activity on your Mac.) You can further refine sorting by telling Sortio to organize things by file type, project, date, and whether the file is for work or personal use..

I took Sortio for a spin, having it go through the folder of articles I’ve written but haven’t bothered to organize for myself. Sortio was smart enough to take my submissions to Awful Announcing and separate them into their own folder. Not every search is that precise — a separate sorting session had Sortio tagging an offer letter from an old employer named Purch as a financial document — but there are edit buttons to correct mislabeled and misfiled material.

You can try out Sortio for free, which gives you enough of an allowance to sort through a few thousand files to get a flavor for how the app performs. After that, you’ll need to buy a license, with the $14.99/month Pro license suitable for most individual users. There are team and enterprise options as well, and paying for an annual license lowers your monthly rate.

AskPlay

AI isn’t just for organizing your folders; it can also generate a playlist for you based on specific artists, songs or moods you’re hoping to hear. At least, that’s the idea behind AskPlay, an app that lives in your menu bar and lets you type or speak plain-English instructions on the type of music you want to listen to.

You’re going to need a few things besides AskPlay and its $1.99/month subscription to make the app work. For starters, AskPlay works exclusively with Apple Music, so you’ll also need to subscribe to Apple’s streaming service. In addition, you’ll need to provide an API key from an AI provider, with AskPlay supporting OpenAI, Anthropic, and OpenRouter.

Those requirements are likely to limit AskPlay’s appeal to some users, but having tried out the app on my Mac, I am impressed by the results. I told AskPlay I wanted to hear songs written by Stephen Sondheim, and it dutifully produced a playlist not just from cast soundtracks but also numbers by vocalists from their own albums.

That said, there were a few misfires — the playlist included a song from Tick, Tick… Boom! , a Jonathan Larson musical that only refers to Sondheim, as well as a rap song that shares a title with something Sondheim wrote. Other requests like “play upbeat songs from the ’80s” proved more successful.

An AskPlay feature I appreciate was the ability to augment playlists. After generating a playlist of Merle Haggard songs, I had the app add Johnny Cash music to the queue. Then I told AskPlay to “add more songs like these,” which brought Waylon Jennings, George Jones, and more to the party.

AskPlay seems built for a very specific kind of user, but if you like thematic playlists and already subscribe to the services that make this app tick, it brings another dimension to your listening experience. In addition to working on the Mac, AskPlay is available for a range of Apple devices including the iPhone, iPad and Vision Pro.

Pocket Screen

I don’t know about you, but my workflow often requires me to jump from one window to another to perform a task — and that can often break up my workflow. I’m thinking of when I’m writing something and need to refer to notes I’ve taken in another application or a PDF I have loaded up in Preview. Jumping between apps takes me out of the flow of writing, not to mention that accurately transcribing what’s in one app to the other can occasionally be a hit-or-miss proposition.

Pocket Screen addresses some of that dilemma by creating a floating window of one app that you can keep in view when you’re working on something else. Think of Pocket Screen as a picture-in-picture feature, but for productivity. You can capture a PDF, webpage, video, chat or other kind of information and keep it close at hand in a resizable window that you can move around your desktop. The app supports up to two simultaneous views, according to its developer.

articles.title: Tetris Distances Itself From Racist White House Clone: ‘We Take Copyright Infringement Very Seriously’
articles.subtitle: Trump’s White House recently added an “arcade” to its website that includes seemingly vibe-coded MAGA rip-offs of well-known games. One of them is called Build the Wall and is an obvious clone of Tetris.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Trump’s White House recently added an “arcade” to its website that includes seemingly vibe-coded MAGA rip-offs of well-known games. One of them is called Build the Wall and is an obvious clone of Tetris. The Tetris Company, which owns the rights to the game, has since come out to disavow the White House’s latest stunt and threaten a potential copyright claim against the administration.

“At Tetris we believe in the power of connection and bringing people together, not dividing them,” the holding company, owned jointly by Tetris creator Alexey Pajitnov and businessman Henk Rogers, wrote on Instagram on September 4. “To our fans everywhere, we love you, we see you, and we’re grateful to have you in our community.”

It added in a follow-up comment on the post, “P.S. The Tetris Company was not involved in the creation of ‘Build the Wall.’ P.P.S. We take copyright infringement very seriously.” The comments are full of people begging The Tetris Company to sue Trump.

If Pajitnov and Rogers ended up doing that, it would be the first instance of a video game company actually taking action against the White House for the unauthorized use of copyrighted gaming material for political memes and other messaging online. Previous shitposts by the president’s staff have included AI edits of Persona 5, Halo ads for ICE, and a MAGA remix of the Pokémon theme song.

“We are aware of recent social content that includes imagery associated with our brand,” Pokémon Company spokeswoman Sravanthi Dev said in an attempt by the company to distance itself from the stunt back in March. “We were not involved in its creation or distribution, and no permission was granted for the use of our intellectual property. Our mission is to bring the world together, and that mission is not affiliated with any political viewpoint or agenda.”

Six months later, no action has been taken, even as Japanese officials reportedly lobby behind the scenes to try to get Trump’s team to stop using video games and anime in its social media posts. So far, they’re all cowards.

articles.content:
Deals on brand new condition M5 MacBook Air models have popped up here and there, but they have been largely intermittent since the price increase a couple months back. Today, however, as part of its Labor Day sale, Amazon is offering this Midnight 13-inch model at $150 off the list price.

Amazon is now offering the 13-inch M5 MacBook Air with 16GB of RAM and the 1TB storage capacity down at $1,449 shipped.

This is the Midnight model that regularly catches a $1,599 list price from Apple and other retailers. Today Amazon has dropped the price to deliver a solid $150 in savings and some notable price increase relief.

There are no signs the price increases are going anywhere, any time soon, if ever. Catching one of the more affordable configurations with a solid $150 price drop in brand new condition is very much notable – these sorts of deals have, by in large, only landed on the Sky Blue configs, and even those deals have been rare and short-lived.

We do not expect this $150 price drop to last for very long as it is the only 13-inch configuration at better than $100 off and most of them aren’t on sale at all.
